client: I just don't feel like doing anything since Max passed away last month. Even going for walks in our favorite park just makes me miss him more. I know it's just a dog, but I can't seem to shake this heavy feeling.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying a deep sense of loss, and even the things that used to bring you joy now feel painful. Grief doesn't measure love by species—it's completely valid to feel this way about Max.  

What thoughts come up when you notice that heavy feeling during your walks?

client: I keep thinking about how empty the house feels now without Max's paws clicking on the floors. Sometimes I'll turn a corner expecting to see him there, and when he's not...it's like getting punched in the chest all over again. I know people say "it's just a dog," but he was my family for 14 years—I don't know how to adjust to this quiet.
therapist:
That anticipatory grief when you turn a corner is so visceral—it's like your heart keeps relearning the loss anew each time. Fourteen years of companionship creates deep neural pathways that don't just disappear.  

When those moments of expectation happen, do you notice any particular thoughts that follow the initial wave of sadness?

client:
It's like my brain still expects to see her waiting by the door when I come home. Then when she's not there, I immediately think "I should have taken her to the vet sooner" or "Maybe if I'd noticed the symptoms earlier..." The guilt hits almost as hard as the sadness itself. 

I know logically that she lived a long life, but in those moments it feels like I failed her somehow. The what-ifs just keep circling in my head.
therapist:
The "what-ifs" can be especially cruel in grief—they take the love you had for Max and twist it into self-blame when you're already hurting. That gap between logical knowing and emotional feeling is so wide right now.  

When those guilty thoughts arise, what helps you reconnect with the truth that you gave Max a lifetime of care?

client:
I know logically that I took good care of Max, but emotionally it still feels like I should have done more. The what-ifs keep haunting me—what if I'd noticed the symptoms sooner, what if I'd taken him to a different vet? It's like my brain won't let me accept that I did enough. 

When you ask what helps me reconnect with the truth... honestly, nothing really does right now. The guilt just feels stronger than any comforting thoughts I try to have.
therapist:
It sounds like the guilt has created a sort of emotional blockade, where even the facts about your good care can't quite penetrate right now. That stuck feeling is so common in grief—the mind keeps returning to the pain like a tongue probing a sore tooth.  

Would it feel possible right now to simply notice those "what-if" thoughts as they come, without trying to argue with them or make them go away? Just observing how they come and go in your mind?

client:
I get what you're saying about observing the thoughts, but it's hard not to argue with them when they feel so urgent and true. Every time I try to just notice them, it's like my brain screams "But what if you HAD done more?" and then I'm right back in that guilty spiral. 

It feels impossible to just watch those thoughts when they carry so much emotional weight behind them. Like if I don't wrestle with them, doesn't that mean I don't care enough?
therapist:
That urgency you describe—where the thoughts demand to be wrestled with—makes complete sense when we're grieving someone we loved so deeply. It's as if your mind believes that by not engaging with the guilt, you're somehow betraying your love for Max.  

What if we tried something different? When that "what if" thought appears, could you imagine placing it gently aside just for a moment, like setting down a heavy object you've been carrying too long? Not to dismiss it, but to give your arms—your heart—a brief rest?

client:
I get what you're saying about setting the thought aside, but it feels wrong somehow. Like if I stop thinking about Max even for a minute, it means I didn't love him enough. The guilt is the only thing keeping me connected to him now. 

And honestly, when I try to put the thoughts down, they just come back louder. It's like they're screaming "how dare you ignore me" when I attempt to take a break. Does that make sense?
therapist:
What you're describing makes complete sense—it's as if the pain has become a sacred bond with Max, and letting go of it even briefly feels like risking that connection. Grief can convince us that suffering equals love.  

When those thoughts come back louder, could we try meeting them with curiosity rather than resistance? Like saying to yourself, "Ah, there's that protective part of me that's afraid to let go of the pain"? How does that land for you?

client:
I get what you're saying about grief making pain feel like love, but it's hard to even imagine trying to be curious about these thoughts. When they hit, it just feels like a wave of guilt—like if I'm not hurting, I'm forgetting him or betraying him somehow. 

The idea of talking to myself about "protective parts" feels too detached. It's not some abstract part of me—it's my whole heart screaming that I failed him.
therapist:
That raw, all-consuming feeling of your heart screaming—that's the depth of your love speaking, not a failure. What if we didn't try to change or analyze those thoughts right now, but simply made space for them to exist alongside your memories of Max's happy moments?  

When the guilt feels most overwhelming, what happens if you let one good memory sit with it—not to replace the pain, but to walk beside it?

client: I guess I can try that, but it feels like letting the guilt coexist with happy memories might just make the pain worse. When I think about Max’s happy moments, it reminds me how much I failed him—like those moments are tainted because I wasn’t good enough. I don’t know if I can separate the guilt from the good memories. It all feels tangled together.
therapist:
That tangled feeling—where love and guilt weave together so tightly—shows just how deeply this loss has shaken your world. It's not about forcing them apart, but noticing how both can exist in the same breath: the warmth of the memories and the ache of missing him.  

When a happy memory surfaces and the guilt tries to claim it, could you pause and ask yourself: "Would Max have wanted me to remember our time together this way?" What comes up when you imagine that?

client:
I know Max wouldn't want me to feel guilty about the happy memories...but that just makes me feel worse somehow. Like I'm failing him by not being able to enjoy them properly. The thought of him wanting me to be happy just adds another layer of pressure. 

It's like my brain twists everything - even his kindness becomes another reason to beat myself up. I try to pause like you suggest, but then the sadness just overwhelms me.
therapist:
It sounds like even the idea of honoring Max’s kindness feels like another weight to carry—as if your grief is caught in a loop where every thought leads back to pain. That overwhelm is so valid when the loss is still so fresh.  

What if, instead of trying to pause or fix anything, you simply let yourself feel whatever comes up in those moments—whether it’s sadness, guilt, or even a flicker of warmth—without judgment? How does that idea sit with you?

client:
I don't know if I can just let myself feel it all without judgment. Every time I start to feel that warmth from remembering Max's kindness, it immediately twists into guilt because I didn't appreciate him enough when he was here. The sadness feels bottomless, like if I really let myself feel it, I might never stop crying. 

I guess part of me is scared that if I stop judging these feelings, it means I'm letting myself off the hook too easily. Does that make sense? Like the pain is the only thing connecting me to him now.
therapist:
That fear makes so much sense—as if easing the pain might somehow dilute your love for Max or dishonor his memory. Grief can make us believe we must keep paying in sorrow for the love we were lucky enough to receive.  

When you notice that fear of "letting yourself off the hook," could you imagine Max nudging your hand with his nose, the way he might have when you were being too hard on yourself before? What might that version of him—who knew your love so deeply—want to tell you right now?
